title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
description: Class 11 Physics (NCERT) notes on centre of mass, torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum and rolling motion, with solved numericals, quizzes and tests.

topics.title: Centre of Mass
topics.concept:
A rigid body has countless particles, yet it moves as if its entire mass were concentrated at a single point. That point is the centre of mass (CM). When you throw a spanner, every particle follows a complicated path, but one special point traces a neat parabola — exactly the path a single particle of the same mass would follow. Studying that point lets us treat an extended body like a point particle.

For a system of discrete particles of masses $m_1, m_2, \dots, m_n$ at position vectors $\vec{r}_1, \vec{r}_2, \dots, \vec{r}_n$, the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position:

  • $\vec{r}_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}=\frac{m_1\vec{r}_1+m_2\vec{r}_2+\cdots+m_n\vec{r}_n}{m_1+m_2+\cdots+m_n}$.
  • In components: $x_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}$ and $y_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i y_i}{\sum m_i}$.
  • For a continuous body the sums become integrals: $\vec{r}_{cm}=\frac{1}{M}\int \vec{r}\,dm$.

For symmetric, uniform bodies the CM lies at the geometric centre. The CM of a uniform rod is at its midpoint, of a uniform disc or ring at its centre, and of a uniform sphere at its centre. Note that the CM need not lie inside the body — for a ring it lies in the empty central space, and for an L-shaped lamina it can fall outside the material altogether.

Motion of the centre of mass. Differentiating $\vec{r}_{cm}$ gives the velocity and acceleration of the CM:

  • $\vec{v}_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{v}_i}{M}$, so the total momentum of the system is $\vec{P}=M\vec{v}_{cm}$.
  • $M\vec{a}_{cm}=\vec{F}_{ext}$ — the CM accelerates only under the net external force; internal forces cancel in pairs (Newton's third law).

Momentum of a system. Because internal forces cannot shift the CM, if $\vec{F}_{ext}=0$ then $\vec{P}=M\vec{v}_{cm}$ is constant — the law of conservation of linear momentum. This is why a bomb exploding in mid-air has fragments flying apart, yet their CM keeps moving along the original parabola: the explosive forces are purely internal.

examples.problem: Two particles of masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed on the x-axis at $x=0$ and $x=5$ m. Find the position of the centre of mass.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $x_{cm}=\frac{m_1 x_1+m_2 x_2}{m_1+m_2}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $x_{cm}=\frac{2(0)+3(5)}{2+3}=\frac{15}{5}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $x_{cm}=3\ \text{m}$.

Answer: The CM is at $x=3\ \text{m}$ (closer to the heavier 3 kg mass).

examples.problem: Three masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are placed at the corners of a triangle: $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ m respectively. Find the coordinates of the centre of mass.
Two particles of masses 4 kg and 6 kg are separated by a distance of 10 m. How far from the 4 kg mass is the centre of mass?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Take the 4 kg mass at $x=0$ and the 6 kg mass at $x=10$ m.
  2. Step 2: $x_{cm}=\frac{4(0)+6(10)}{4+6}=\frac{60}{10}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $x_{cm}=6\ \text{m}$ from the 4 kg mass.

Answer: $6\ \text{m}$ from the 4 kg mass (i.e. 4 m from the 6 kg mass).

examples.problem: A particle of mass 2 kg moves with velocity $3\ \text{m/s}$ and another of mass 1 kg moves with velocity $6\ \text{m/s}$ in the same direction. Find the velocity of the centre of mass.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $v_{cm}=\frac{m_1 v_1+m_2 v_2}{m_1+m_2}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $v_{cm}=\frac{2(3)+1(6)}{2+1}=\frac{12}{3}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $v_{cm}=4\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $v_{cm}=4\ \text{m/s}$ in the same direction.

examples.problem: A shell of mass 5 kg moving at $10\ \text{m/s}$ explodes into two fragments. One fragment of mass 2 kg flies off at $25\ \text{m/s}$ in the original direction. Find the velocity of the other fragment.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Total momentum is conserved (only internal forces act): $P_i=5\times10=50\ \text{kg m/s}$.
  2. Step 2: After explosion: $P_f=2(25)+3(v)=50+3v$.
  3. Step 3: Set $50=50+3v\Rightarrow v=0$. The 3 kg fragment momentarily comes to rest.

Answer: The 3 kg fragment has velocity $0\ \text{m/s}$ (it stops).

examples.problem: Two masses of 1 kg are at $(0,0)$ and $(4,0)$ m. A third mass is added at $(4,3)$ m so that the CM lies at $(2,1)$ m. Find the third mass.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $y_{cm}=\frac{m_1 y_1+m_2 y_2+m_3 y_3}{m_1+m_2+m_3}$ with the y-values $0,0,3$.
  2. Step 2: $1=\frac{1(0)+1(0)+m_3(3)}{1+1+m_3}=\frac{3m_3}{2+m_3}$.
  3. Step 3: Solve: $2+m_3=3m_3\Rightarrow 2=2m_3\Rightarrow m_3=1\ \text{kg}$.

Answer: The third mass is $1\ \text{kg}$.

recap: Centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean position: $\vec{r}_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$.
For uniform symmetric bodies the CM is at the geometric centre and may lie outside the material (e.g. a ring).
Total momentum of a system equals $\vec{P}=M\vec{v}_{cm}$.
The CM accelerates only under the net external force: $M\vec{a}_{cm}=\vec{F}_{ext}$; internal forces cancel.
If $\vec{F}_{ext}=0$, total momentum is conserved and the CM moves with constant velocity.

options: mass-weighted average position of all particles
geometric midpoint of the outline only
quiz.explanation: By definition $\vec{r}_{cm}=\frac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$, the mass-weighted mean position.

quiz.q: Two masses 2 kg and 8 kg are 10 m apart. The CM lies:
quiz.explanation: $x_{cm}$ measured from 8 kg $=\frac{2\times10}{10}=2\ \text{m}$; it is closer to the heavier mass.

quiz.q: The centre of mass of a uniform ring lies:
options: at the centre, in the empty space
quiz.explanation: By symmetry the CM is at the geometric centre, which contains no material.

quiz.q: When a shell explodes in mid-air, the centre of mass of the fragments:
quiz.explanation: Explosive forces are internal; the only external force is gravity, so the CM keeps its projectile path.

topics.title: Torque, Moment of Inertia & Angular Momentum
topics.concept:
Force makes things move; torque makes things turn. The turning effect of a force about an axis is called torque (or moment of force). It depends not just on how hard you push, but on where and in what direction you push. That is why a door opens easily at the handle but barely budges near the hinge.

Torque is the cross product of the position vector $\vec{r}$ (from the axis to the point of application) and the force $\vec{F}$:

  • $\vec{\tau}=\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, with magnitude $\tau=rF\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$.
  • $\tau=F\times(r\sin\theta)=F\times d$, where $d=r\sin\theta$ is the lever arm (perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force).
  • The SI unit of torque is the newton metre ($\text{N m}$); its direction is along the axis of rotation (right-hand rule).

Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass — it measures a body's resistance to angular acceleration. For a system of particles it is the mass-weighted sum of the squares of distances from the axis:

  • $I=\sum m_i r_i^2$ (continuous body: $I=\int r^2\,dm$). SI unit: $\text{kg m}^2$.
  • It depends on the total mass and how that mass is distributed about the axis — mass far from the axis contributes much more.
  • Standard results: thin ring/hoop about its axis $I=MR^2$; solid disc/cylinder about its axis $I=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$; solid sphere about a diameter $I=\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$; thin rod about its centre $I=\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$.

Radius of gyration $k$ is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia: $I=Mk^2$, so $k=\sqrt{I/M}$.

Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum. For a particle $\vec{L}=\vec{r}\times\vec{p}$, and for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis $L=I\omega$ (SI unit $\text{kg m}^2\text{/s}$). When the net external torque is zero, $\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}=\vec{\tau}_{ext}=0$, so angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$. An ice-skater spins faster by pulling the arms in (reducing $I$, raising $\omega$) — a direct demonstration of this law.

examples.problem: A force of 20 N is applied at the end of a wrench 0.25 m long, perpendicular to it. Find the torque about the bolt.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\tau=rF\sin\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$, so $\sin\theta=1$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\tau=0.25\times20\times1$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\tau=5\ \text{N m}$.

Answer: $\tau=5\ \text{N m}$.

examples.problem: A force of 50 N acts at a point 0.4 m from the axis, making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the position vector. Find the torque.
Two point masses of 2 kg each are fixed at the ends of a light rod of length 2 m. Find the moment of inertia about an axis through the centre, perpendicular to the rod.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Each mass is at $r=1$ m from the centre.
  2. Step 2: $I=\sum m_i r_i^2=2(1)^2+2(1)^2$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $I=2+2=4\ \text{kg m}^2$.

Answer: $I=4\ \text{kg m}^2$.

examples.problem: A solid disc has mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m. Find its moment of inertia about the central axis, and its radius of gyration.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a disc $I=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2=\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(0.5)^2$.
  2. Step 2: Compute: $I=\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(0.25)=0.5\ \text{kg m}^2$.
  3. Step 3: Radius of gyration $k=\sqrt{I/M}=\sqrt{0.5/4}=\sqrt{0.125}$.

Answer: $I=0.5\ \text{kg m}^2$ and $k\approx0.354\ \text{m}$.

examples.problem: A disc of moment of inertia $0.2\ \text{kg m}^2$ rotates at an angular speed of $10\ \text{rad/s}$. Find its angular momentum.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $L=I\omega$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $L=0.2\times10$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $L=2\ \text{kg m}^2\text{/s}$.

Answer: $L=2\ \text{kg m}^2\text{/s}$.

examples.problem: A skater spinning at $2\ \text{rev/s}$ with moment of inertia $4\ \text{kg m}^2$ pulls in the arms, reducing the moment of inertia to $1\ \text{kg m}^2$. Find the new rate of spin.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: No external torque, so angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$.
  2. Step 2: $\omega_2=\frac{I_1\omega_1}{I_2}=\frac{4\times2}{1}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\omega_2=8\ \text{rev/s}$.

Answer: The skater spins at $8\ \text{rev/s}$ (four times faster).

recap: Torque is the turning effect of a force: $\vec{\tau}=\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, magnitude $\tau=rF\sin\theta=Fd$.
Moment of inertia is rotational mass: $I=\sum m_i r_i^2$; it depends on mass distribution about the axis.
Standard results: ring $MR^2$, disc $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$, rod (centre) $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$.
Angular momentum $L=I\omega$; if net external torque is zero, $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$ (conservation).

quiz.q: The torque produced by a force is maximum when the angle between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$ is:
The moment of inertia of a thin ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is:
quiz.explanation: All the mass of a ring lies at distance $R$ from the axis, so $I=MR^2$.

quiz.q: The rotational analogue of linear momentum is:
quiz.explanation: Angular momentum $L=I\omega$ corresponds to linear momentum $p=mv$.

quiz.q: An ice-skater pulls in the arms while spinning. The angular speed:
quiz.explanation: With no external torque, $L=I\omega$ is constant; reducing $I$ increases $\omega$.

topics.title: Rotational Dynamics & Rolling
topics.concept:
Just as $F=ma$ governs straight-line motion, an exactly parallel law governs rotation. A net torque produces angular acceleration in direct proportion to the torque and inversely to the moment of inertia. This makes rotational dynamics a near-perfect mirror of translational dynamics — every linear quantity has a rotational twin.

The rotational equation of motion is:

  • $\tau=I\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration ($\text{rad/s}^2$) — the rotational analogue of $F=ma$.
  • The work done by a torque through an angle $\theta$ is $W=\tau\theta$, and the power delivered is $P=\tau\omega$.
  • Rotational kinetic energy: a body rotating with angular speed $\omega$ stores energy $KE_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, the analogue of $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
  • Work–energy theorem for rotation: $W_{net}=\Delta KE_{rot}=\frac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2-\frac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2$.

Rolling without slipping combines translation of the centre of mass with rotation about it. The key condition is that the contact point is instantaneously at rest, which links the two motions:

  • $v=\omega R$ (velocity of the centre) and $a=\alpha R$ (acceleration), where $R$ is the radius.
  • The total kinetic energy is the sum of translational and rotational parts: $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2+\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.
  • Using $I=mk^2$ and $v=\omega R$, this becomes $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1+\frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$.

Rolling down an incline. When a body rolls (without slipping) down a slope of height $h$, the lost potential energy $mgh$ becomes shared between translational and rotational KE. Solving energy conservation gives the speed at the bottom and the acceleration along the incline:

  • $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1+\frac{k^2}{R^2}}}$ and $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+\frac{k^2}{R^2}}$.
  • Because $\frac{k^2}{R^2}$ is smallest for a sphere ($\tfrac{2}{5}$), larger for a disc ($\tfrac{1}{2}$), and largest for a ring ($1$), a solid sphere reaches the bottom first, then the disc, then the ring — regardless of mass or radius.

examples.problem: A torque of $6\ \text{N m}$ acts on a flywheel of moment of inertia $3\ \text{kg m}^2$. Find the angular acceleration.
A disc of moment of inertia $0.5\ \text{kg m}^2$ rotates at $4\ \text{rad/s}$. Find its rotational kinetic energy.
A wheel of radius 0.4 m rolls without slipping with a centre speed of $6\ \text{m/s}$. Find its angular speed.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For rolling without slipping $v=\omega R$, so $\omega=\frac{v}{R}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\omega=\frac{6}{0.4}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\omega=15\ \text{rad/s}$.

Answer: $\omega=15\ \text{rad/s}$.

examples.problem: A solid sphere of mass 2 kg rolls without slipping at $3\ \text{m/s}$. Find its total kinetic energy. (For a solid sphere $\frac{k^2}{R^2}=\frac{2}{5}$.)
A disc rolls without slipping from rest down an incline of height 2.1 m. Find the speed at the bottom. (For a disc $\frac{k^2}{R^2}=\frac{1}{2}$, $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.)
A ring and a solid sphere of the same mass and radius roll down the same incline from rest. Which reaches the bottom first, and why?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+\frac{k^2}{R^2}}$; a larger $\frac{k^2}{R^2}$ gives a smaller acceleration.
  2. Step 2: For the ring $\frac{k^2}{R^2}=1$; for the solid sphere $\frac{k^2}{R^2}=\frac{2}{5}$.
  3. Step 3: The sphere has the smaller $\frac{k^2}{R^2}$, so the larger acceleration, independent of mass and radius.

Answer: The solid sphere reaches the bottom first.

recap: Rotational Newton's law: $\tau=I\alpha$; work $W=\tau\theta$ and power $P=\tau\omega$.
Rolling without slipping requires $v=\omega R$ and $a=\alpha R$.
Down an incline $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}$; the solid sphere beats the disc, which beats the ring.

quiz.explanation: Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration: $\tau=I\alpha$.

quiz.q: The rotational kinetic energy of a body is:
For a wheel rolling without slipping, the velocity of the centre is:
quiz.explanation: The rolling condition (contact point at rest) gives $v=\omega R$.

quiz.q: A solid sphere, a disc and a ring roll down the same incline from rest. The first to reach the bottom is the:
quiz.explanation: The sphere has the smallest $k^2/R^2$ ($\tfrac{2}{5}$), so the largest acceleration, independent of mass and radius.
